primer.intro: A heap is a complete binary tree that lives inside a flat array - no pointers, just index arithmetic. The element at index i has its children at 2i+1 and 2i+2 and its parent at the floor of (i-1)/2. A min-heap adds one promise: every parent is at most its children, so the root is always the minimum. Notice how much weaker that is than a search tree's promise - siblings are in no particular order, and the array as a whole is anything but sorted. That weakness is the point. By promising less, the heap repairs itself faster: insertion and removal cost one root-to-leaf journey, and turning an arbitrary array into a heap costs plain linear time.
whenToUse: You repeatedly need the smallest (or largest) of a set that keeps changing.
Top-k questions: the kth largest, the k best, with far fewer than n slots of memory.
Merging k sorted lists or streams into one sorted output.
Nearly-sorted data, each element at most k positions adrift - a size k+1 heap tidies it in one pass.
primer.mentalModel: Two repair moves run the whole machine. Sift up: a newcomer appended at the end bubbles toward the root while it beats its parent - that is insertion. Sift down: when the root is removed, the last element takes its place and sinks, swapping with its smaller child until both children are bigger - that is extraction. Building a heap composes sift-downs bottom-up, from the last internal node (index n/2 - 1) back to the root: leaves are already heaps, deep nodes sift short distances, and the costs sum to linear, beating n separate insertions. For top-k, flip the instinct: the kth largest is guarded by a min-heap of size k whose root is the current threshold - beat the root to get in, and the root is the answer.
mistakes: Reading the heap array as sorted - only the root is promised; the rest is a controlled jumble.
Building by sifting down from index 0 forward; a sift-down assumes the subtrees below are already heaps.
Guarding the kth largest with a max-heap of size k that evicts its maximum - that keeps the k smallest instead.

example.title: Sift down, the heap's repair move
example.explain: The two comparisons find the smallest among the node and its children; if the node already wins, the subtree is a heap and the loop ends. Otherwise the node swaps with its smaller child - swapping with the larger one would put a big value above a small one and break the promise sideways. Build-heap runs this from the last internal node back to the root; extraction runs it once from the root after the swap with the last element.

primer.practice: Open Practice with Check if an Array Represents a Min-Heap - it is pure index arithmetic and burns the 2i+1, 2i+2 reflex in.

sections.title: The array is the tree
sections.text: The completeness rule - every level full, the last one filled left to right - is what lets the tree flatten into an array with no gaps and no pointers. Index 0 is the root; children of i sit at 2i+1 and 2i+2; the parent of j is the floor of (j-1)/2; the last internal node is at n/2 - 1, and everything after it is a leaf. Checking the heap promise is one loop over the internal nodes comparing each with its children. Keep the picture honest: the promise flows only parent to child, so cousins and siblings may be in any order, and finding an arbitrary element still costs a full scan.

check.prompt: In the array view of a heap, which index is the parent of index 7, and where do index 7's own children sit?

options.explain: Neighbouring indices are cousins, left and right in the same level.
Children start at 2i+1, so 15 - index 14 belongs to node 6.
(7-1)/2 floors to 3; index 4 parents 9 and 10.
Floor of (7-1)/2 is 3, and 2*7+1, 2*7+2 give 15 and 16.

reveal.solution: Run the formulas. Parent of j: floor of (j-1)/2 = floor of 6/2 = 3. Children of i: 2i+1 and 2i+2 = 15 and 16. The inverse pair of formulas is the entire pointer structure of a heap - no node objects, no links, just multiplication and division by two, which is also why heaps are so cache-friendly in practice.

sections.title: Top-k with a small heap
sections.text: To track the kth largest of a stream, keep a min-heap holding the k largest values seen so far. Its root is the smallest of those champions - the threshold. A newcomer either fails to beat the root and is discarded, or replaces it: push, and pop the minimum if the size spills past k. At every moment the root is the kth largest so far, and each arrival costs log k, with k slots of memory regardless of the stream's length. The same shape sorts a k-sorted array: push the first k+1 elements, then pop-push along the array - the minimum of that small window is always the next output - and merges k sorted lists by keeping one head per list in the heap.

quiz.prompt: A stream keeps arriving and you must always know the kth largest so far. Which tool?

options.explain: Every arrival pays a full insertion into n elements, and memory grows forever.
Finding the kth means popping k times per query, then pushing back.
Two numbers cannot represent the k-frontier in between.

options.text: A min-heap capped at k values; its root is the answer
options.explain: The heap guards the k champions; the smallest of them is exactly the kth largest.

quiz.prompt: Merge k sorted lists into one sorted output. What belongs in the heap?

options.text: All elements of all lists at once
options.explain: Works, but n log n beats nothing; the k-head version costs n log k.
Lengths say how much is left, nothing about which value comes next.

options.text: Only the first list, then merge pairwise
options.explain: Pairwise merging re-touches elements log k times without a heap's guidance.

options.text: One current head per list - pop the smallest, push its successor
options.explain: The overall next element is always the smallest of the k heads.

quiz.prompt: Every element sits at most k positions from its sorted place. How is the array sorted cheaply?

options.text: A min-heap over a sliding window of k+1 elements; pop one, push the next
options.explain: The true next element must be inside the window, so each pop emits correctly.
Correct, but n log n ignores the promise; the window heap costs n log k.
Up to k passes of n - the quadratic road.
Direction changes nothing about the work.

quiz.prompt: A changing set needs repeated extract-the-minimum. Why a heap over a sorted array?

options.text: Sorted arrays cannot extract the minimum
options.explain: They can - it sits at one end; insertion is what hurts them.

options.text: Heap insert and extract both cost log n; the sorted array pays linear per insert
options.explain: Shifting elements to keep an array sorted is the hidden linear bill.

options.text: The heap keeps everything sorted too
options.explain: It keeps far less - one promise per edge - which is exactly why it is faster.
Arbitrary search in a heap is a full scan; only the root is instant.

quiz.prompt: Does the array 10 20 30 21 23 satisfy the min-heap promise?

options.text: It fails because the array is unsorted
options.explain: Heap order is parent-child only; sortedness is a stronger, different thing.

options.text: Yes - 10 is under 20 and 30; 20 is under 21 and 23
options.explain: Both internal nodes beat their children; leaves have nothing to prove.
Siblings carry no promise between them - any order is fine.
30 and 21 are in different subtrees; no edge connects them.

quiz.prompt: Bottom-up build-heap (min) runs on 5 4 3 2 1. What array results?

options.explain: Sift at index 1 swaps 4 with 1; sift at 0 sinks 5 via 1's slot, then past 2.
Build-heap repairs the promise; it does nothing as strong as sorting.
The input breaks the promise everywhere - the build must move things.
After the root sinks, the sift continues down - 5 cannot rest above 2.

quiz.prompt: A size-3 min-heap tracks the 3rd largest of the stream 10, 20, 11, 70. What is reported after 70 arrives?

options.explain: 20 is the 2nd largest; the root sits one below it.
The champions are 70, 20, 11; the heap's root 11 is the 3rd largest.
10 was evicted when 70 pushed the heap past three.
70 is the 1st largest; the root holds the smallest champion, the kth.

quiz.prompt: Why does bottom-up build-heap cost linear time, beating n single insertions?

options.text: Most nodes sit near the bottom and sift short distances; the sum telescopes to O(n)
options.explain: Half the nodes are leaves costing zero; costs shrink geometrically going down.
A single sift can travel the whole height; it is the distribution that saves the total.
Leaves are skipped as sift starts, but they are still part of the heap.

options.text: It is actually n log n, just fast in practice
options.explain: The telescoped bound is genuinely linear - this is the classic surprise.

quiz.prompt: Tracking the kth largest over a stream of n items with a size-k min-heap costs?

options.text: n log k time and k memory
options.explain: Each arrival pays one heap operation on k elements, with k slots held.

options.text: n log n time and n memory
options.explain: That is the keep-everything plan the capped heap replaces.
The heap replaces the linear scan of the champions with a log k repair.
The repair walk costs log k - tiny, but real.

quiz.prompt: This build-heap leaves 3 above 1 on input 5 4 3 2 1. What is the bug?

options.text: The loop runs top-down; sift-down assumes the subtrees below are already heaps
options.explain: Run i from n/2 - 1 back to 0 so every child subtree is repaired first.

options.text: The bound misses the last leaf
options.explain: Leaves need no sifting - they have no children to violate. The direction is the fault.
Sift-up builds in n log n; the linear build wants sift-down, just bottom-up.
The internal nodes end at n/2 - 1; the range is right, the order is backwards.

quiz.prompt: This kth-largest tracker ends up holding the k smallest values. What is the bug?

options.explain: Speed is fine - it is removing exactly the values worth keeping.

options.text: Evicting the maximum keeps the small; a min-heap evicting its minimum keeps the champions
options.explain: The guardian must discard its weakest champion, the root of a min-heap.

options.text: The push must come after the size check
options.explain: Push-then-trim is the standard dance; what is trimmed is the fault.
Size k is correct for the kth largest; the eviction policy is backwards.

quiz.prompt: Which case most deserves a dedicated test for a kth-largest routine?

options.explain: The comfortable case - nothing boundary-shaped happens.
Small but unremarkable; the k = n and k = 1 extremes work harder.
Length stresses time, but the k = n boundary stresses correctness.

options.text: k equal to the array's length
options.explain: The answer is the minimum, the heap fills completely, and off-by-ones surface.
